newsitem.title: CANADA: Ottawa meeting set to launch Zaire rescue mission.
newsitem.headline: Ottawa meeting set to launch Zaire rescue mission.

text.p: A Canadian-led meeting in Ottawa was set on Friday to give final approval to a scaled-down force to help refugees in eastern Zaire.
Ambassadors from participating nations were to meet to give formal approval to the establishment of a military headquarters in Entebbe, Uganda, as well as reconnaissance missions and airdrops.

The expected authorisation comes nearly three weeks after Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien began telephoning world leaders to rescue what aid agencies then said were more than a million refugees and displaced people in eastern Zaire.
Since then about 600,000 refugees have returned to Rwanda, but Western officials have identified at least 200,000 more and believe there could be hundreds of thousands of others.

"Reports of continued human suffering indicate we need to be prepared if more help is needed," Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said on Thursday afternoon as he announced agreement from more than 20 countries to go ahead.

Foreign affairs spokesman John Bell said fewer than 20 nations would be represented at the "steering board" meeting in Ottawa but all the major contributing nations would be there. He added that the agreement had held overnight since Axworthy made his announcement.
The meeting was due to end around 3 p.m. EST 2000 GMT, after which the mission could in theory begin, Bell said. The force would be much smaller than the 10,000 Chretien had originally envisaged.

Controversy has centred on a plan to drop food by air, given the reluctance of Rwandan government to allow a military force to operate from Rwanda or for humanitarian agencies to cross into Zaire from Rwanda.

"Of course we all would like to see a more advanced support, of convoys if that's possible, but we didn't get agreement on that," Axworthy told reporters on Thursday. "The international community was not in consensus that that was necessary at the time."

Asked if the cooperation of neighbouring Rwanda was required for convoys, he said: "That would be one of the questions. I'm hoping in fact from what we've seen today that the Rwandan government is showing more cooperation."

He said the major international relief groups, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, the Red Cross and the World Food Programme, had all agreed to work with and support the idea of food drops, even if some in the region questioned it.

Chretien said during a visit to Japan that Canadian Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril, commander of the international force, had secured agreement in principle on airdrops from the Tutsi rebels that control eastern Zaire.
But Axworthy made clear in his statement that airdrops would be used only "if needed." He added that further reconnaissance would be the first priority to determine exactly where food was needed.
Canada is providing 600 people for the mission, while Senegal has offered 800 troops. Other contributors include the United States, France, Belgium, South Africa, Malawi, Denmark and Japan.
